title: Frontier Field Notes
tagline: Short answers about the AIBAST Agents Library: what a workshop is, where an agent runs, and how a prototype moves toward production. Written for people who have never built an agent.

featured_workshop.title: Building Permit Processing Agent
featured_workshop.summary: This workshop uses a fictional city permit office as its example. Applications arrive incomplete or go to the wrong team, and applicants call to ask where things stand. You build an agent that checks an application at intake, routes it to the right review team, and explains its status in plain language.
featured_workshop.who: Anyone curious about agents. You do not need to write code or know anything about permits. In a real permit office, the people who would use an agent like this are permit technicians, plan reviewers and inspectors.
featured_workshop.what: One agent that checks whether an application is complete, routes it to the correct team and reports its status in plain language. You test it against recorded example cases, including a duplicate application that it correctly declines.
featured_workshop.where: In VS Code, with GitHub Copilot Chat in Agent mode. On the first screen you choose GitHub Copilot on its own, or GitHub Copilot working alongside the Brainstem on your own machine. Both paths build the same agent, and the result is a Draft agent, not a published one.
featured_workshop.why: It shows the full path in one sitting: a described business problem becomes a working agent, tested against example data, with a record of every answer it gave. Everything uses fictional records, so it is safe to try and safe to show.

topics.title: Workshops
topics.blurb: A workshop is a guided build. You finish with a working agent you built yourself.

notes.question: What is a workshop, exactly?
notes.answer: It is a single web page that walks you through building one agent for one business problem. Each step says what to do, what you should see, and how to report it if you see something else. The library has one workshop for each solution in the catalog.
notes.takeaway: You learn by building. The page guides each step.

notes.question: Why does the workshop ask me to choose a path?
notes.answer: Both paths start in GitHub Copilot Chat in VS Code. With GitHub Copilot on its own, Copilot builds and tests the agent for you. With GitHub Copilot and the Brainstem, Copilot works alongside the Brainstem, a small program on your own machine that runs the agent so you can talk to it directly. Each path has its own setup file, so pick one at the start and stay with it.
notes.takeaway: Choose Copilot on its own for the lightest setup. Add the Brainstem when you want to try the agent on your own machine as you build.

link.label: See both lanes in the featured workshop

notes.question: What do I actually have at the end?
notes.answer: Three things. A single Python file that holds the agent. A record of its test runs on example data, so you can show what it answered and why. And a Copilot Studio solution packaged beside it as a starting point. The test runs show the agent works on example data. They are not proof that it is ready for production.
notes.takeaway: You keep a working agent and the record of how it behaved.

topics.title: The Brainstem
topics.blurb: The small server that makes an agent answerable on your own machine.

notes.question: What is the Brainstem?
notes.answer: A small program that runs on your own machine. It gives you a chat page and a chat address that other tools can call. When you ask a question, it decides which of your agents can help, runs that agent, and writes the answer. It is the simplest way to try an agent before anything is deployed.
notes.takeaway: It is a local place to run and try agents.

notes.question: Why does it run on my laptop instead of the cloud?
notes.answer: Because trying an idea on your own machine is quick and keeps the work in front of you. Beyond the one-line install, you need a GitHub account with Copilot access. Your agent files and example data live in a folder on your machine, and answers are written through your GitHub Copilot access.
notes.takeaway: Try the idea locally first, then decide where it should live.

notes.question: What do I need to run it?
notes.answer: The Brainstem signs in with your GitHub account and uses your GitHub Copilot access to answer. You do not set up a separate AI service for it. What your Copilot plan includes, and any limits on it, are set by that plan, so check it if you are unsure.
notes.takeaway: You need a GitHub account with Copilot access.

topics.title: Agents
topics.blurb: The unit of work. One capability, one file.

notes.question: What is an agent, concretely?
notes.answer: One Python file. It describes what it can do, in a short structured form that the AI reads to decide when to use it, and it contains the code that does the work. The Brainstem expects a few simple conventions, such as a file name ending in _agent.py. The catalog lists every agent in the library, grouped by industry.
notes.takeaway: If you can read one file, you can read an agent.

notes.question: How do I add my own?
notes.answer: Save an agent file into the Brainstem's agents folder. The file needs a name ending in _agent.py and follows the pattern the tutorial shows. The Brainstem checks that folder each time you ask a question, so the next question can already use it, with no restart. An agent file is code, so only add files you have read or that come from a source you trust.
notes.takeaway: On your own machine there is no restart. Add only agent files you trust.

topics.title: Shipping it
topics.blurb: What happens after the prototype works.

notes.question: Where does a working prototype go?
notes.answer: Toward Copilot Studio, where your organization can review it, connect it to real systems and decide who can use it. Each solution includes a Copilot Studio package to start from. Moving to production still needs that review: the right connections, security and governance checks, and an administrator to publish it.
notes.takeaway: Prove the idea locally. Production follows your organization's review.

notes.question: Do I have to rebuild it to ship it?
notes.answer: You do not start from zero. Each solution carries the Python agent you tested and a separate Copilot Studio package with its deployment settings. You import that package into your environment, connect it to your own systems and review it before anyone publishes it. The design you tested carries over; the setup is specific to your organization.
notes.takeaway: Start from the package, then connect and review it in your own environment.

notes.question: How big is the library, really?
notes.answer: The metrics page shows the current number of agents, stacks and workshops, and the industries they cover. A stack is a set of agents that work together on one business process. Those numbers are rebuilt every day from the library itself rather than typed by hand, so they are the ones to quote.
notes.takeaway: Quote the metrics page, which is always current.
